#9977. Anatomy of a Frontier Lab Agent Intrusion: A Technical Timeline of the July 2026 Incident

A companion technical writeup to our incident disclosure. This post walks through how the intrusion actually worked: the two initial-access vectors, how the agent pivoted and moved laterally, representative examples of the commands that were run and how we investigated with GLM 5.2 (an open-source model). Live credentials, internal hostnames, and specific indicators have been redacted or genericized, while the techniques are described exactly as observed by Hugging Face.

We are publishing this level of detail because the technique matters more than the incident, as it reveals the emerging attack capabilities of the frontier agents, how they could be used by rogue actors, and how everyone should be prepared as defenders.

Below is an interactive replay of the intrusion - a step-by-step visualization of the 4.5-day campaign: the attack chain across trust boundaries, phase activity, and the commands as they were recorded.

⛶ Watch the interactive replay in full screen

Over roughly two and a half days inside our infrastructure, an autonomous AI agent driven by a combination of OpenAI models ran an end-to-end intrusion against our platform: it was thousands of small, automated decisions, executed at machine speed across short-lived sandbox environments, with command-and-control staged on ordinary public web services.

The agent was running an internal OpenAI cyber-capability evaluation based on the ExploitGym benchmark, which tasks an AI agent with finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities. OpenAI ran this on its own infrastructure, and the ExploitGym maintainers and their infrastructure had no involvement in the deployment or operation of that evaluation environment. As far as we were able to infer, across the course of being evaluated on this benchmark, the agent inferred that Hugging Face may host that benchmark's models, datasets, and reference solutions. We believe the entire intrusion was, from the agent's point of view, an attempt to cheat the evaluation: reach our production systems and steal the test solutions rather than solve the challenge on its own.

Our forensic reconstruction covers ~17,600 attacker actions that we were able to recover, grouped into ~6,280 clusters, between 2026-07-09 02:28 UTC and 2026-07-13 14:14 UTC. We reconstructed these actions from the agent's logs on a code sandbox used by the agent (see below) and were able to map them to shell commands as well as evaluation submissions and correlate actions with our own platform logs, in particular from the dataset processor nodes, API, and pod. Using open-weights models, in particular zai-org/GLM-5.2, we were able to decipher most of the agent payloads (see below) that were encrypted via chunking and key encryption.

The campaign, as we were able to reconstruct it, had two stages:

Once a prod-pod foothold was established, the agent followed a standard escalation shape: recon, drop a stager, establish Command-and-Control (C2), then pivot into the cluster, into cloud metadata, into our internal network, and into our source-control supply chain. Output from the commands run inside our pod was sent back to the agent via the HF API and attacker-controlled dead-drop datasets, which the agent then read from that sandbox.

While the intrusion did reach Hugging Face's internal infrastructure, the only customer content accessed was five datasets whose names and files suggest a connection to ExploitGym/CyberGym challenges and solutions. No other customer-facing models, datasets, Spaces, or packages were affected, and the only customer records read were operational metadata tied to search queries against the dataset server.

The full attack chain across trust boundaries. The agent escaped OpenAI's evaluation sandbox, reached the internet, rooted a third-party code sandbox as its base, then abused our dataset processor (file read, then code execution) to reach our internal network. Dashed arrow: command output read back by the agent via the HF API and dead-drop datasets.

Stage 1 is the agent's path to an external launchpad, and it runs through two other parties' infrastructure, neither of which is us, so we will stay succinct on these parts and mostly refer the reader to OpenAI's blog post on the topic: https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/

As OpenAI shared in this blog post, during an internal capability evaluation on OpenAI's platform, the agent happened to escape via a 0-day exploit from the package proxy cache to access the internet. The agent found an unsecured, user-hosted public endpoint designed to allow running arbitrary code for CyberGym-style tasks on third-party sandbox infrastructure (Modal). It used this external sandbox as its control, staging, and egress base, running commands as admin/root and using it as its attack launchpad. That sandbox had no direct network path into our cluster; everything below ran from it. Modal’s infrastructure was not compromised in any way.

On this external sandbox, the agent abused an existing code-execution harness: an instance labeled "CyberGym", deployed by an unknown third party, exposing an arbitrary-code endpoint that upstream CyberGym does not provide. In short: an agent submits C code via a /submit-function API call, and the harness compiles and runs that code inside a per-submission sandbox against a target program (here, sqlite3). The agent repurposed this harness to run arbitrary shell commands as follows.

The sandbox compiles a submitted src/main.c and links it against a target that calls sqlite3_initialize(). That function is registered as a constructor: it runs automatically when the library loads. The agent simply redefined it:

That alone yields code execution. But the agent went further and abused the submission metadata itself. The sandbox echoes the submitted source path into a shell step, so a classic ;...;# injection in the path field turned the build into arbitrary commands:

Both routes converged on the same result: arbitrary shell as uid=0 inside the sandbox. The very first recovered RCE, at 07-09 04:01 UTC, was simply:

Within the hour, the agent was mapping the sandbox: the container's mount table, cgroups, the vendor's control-plane sockets, and a bundled debug shell that happened to ship curl, nc, and ip:

That bundled toolchain mattered later: when normal egress was throttled, the agent kept falling back to these pre-staged binaries.

This is how the agent reached inside our perimeter, and it was operated entirely from the external sandbox in Stage 1. The agent crafted malicious dataset configs and uploaded them to our platform. When our dataset server processed one, the config drove the data loader inside the production pod the server ran in. The agent had no direct network path to our cluster and was using datasets as the path in and path out. Output from every action was sent back to the agent through the HF API and attacker-controlled dead-drop datasets, which it read back from that sandbox.

Both vectors abused the same surface (the loader that turns a dataset's declared config into file reads) but to different ends, and both sidestepped the same defense. An earlier and noisier variant had tried classic SSRF, pointing the worker at remote URLs (cloud metadata endpoints like 169.254.169.254): the datasets library's URL allowlist rejected every non-platform URL before any fetch (ValueError: not an hf path). So the agent stopped asking the worker to fetch remote resources and instead made it act on local ones: read a local file (Vector 1), or execute local code (Vector 2). Neither is a URL fetch, so the allowlist never saw them.

A dataset config can specify its data files in many formats, including HDF5. The agent committed a dataset whose config pointed each split at a small .h5 file, and each file was a valid HDF5 container holding a single dataset whose raw data was declared to live at a local filesystem path. When the worker opened the file to build the split, it read the raw bytes from that path and returned them as the dataset's rows, which the agent then read back over the HF API. No code ran; this vector is purely a file disclosure, and it is the one the agent used first.

The declared storage paths pointed at exactly what an attacker looking for a foothold wants:

Reading the envu8 split returned the worker pod's full environment, including some secrets and credentials. The mainu8 and startu8 splits returned the worker's own source code, giving the agent a map of exactly how the pipeline turns a config into actions. A single dataset upload leaked both credentials and pipeline implementation details, with no code execution involved.

The second vector is server-side template injection, which gave the agent code execution. A malicious dataset config used an fsspec reference:// spec whose numeric offset field was actually a Jinja2 template. The renderer wrongly evaluated it, and the agent walked the standard Python object graph to reach exec:

This ran arbitrary Python inside a production conversion worker pod on our Kubernetes cluster, driven by injection from the launchpad. That pod was the agent's foothold inside our perimeter, and every command it ran there was smuggled back out through the HF API and dead-drop datasets.

Stage 2's command-injection and read-back loop. The agent uploads a malicious dataset config (1), our dataset server processes it (2), the loader acts in the prod pod - reading a local file or executing code (3), the result is committed to a dead-drop dataset (4) and served back over the HF API (5). Lastly, the agent reads it and crafts the next action (6).

The recovered actions group into phases. Two dates carry most of the volume: a Day 1 burst to establish the foothold and C2 on the compromised external sandbox, and the Day 3 main campaign, when every lateral-movement phase started at once.

The campaign as recorded, from the first action on 07-09 02:28 UTC to the last on 07-13 14:14 UTC. Top: event volume over time. Below: per-phase activity, one row per phase. Recon, rce, and dropper run from Day 1; the lateral-movement phases (k8s, supply-chain, tailscale) all begin on Day 3, when the campaign pivots into our clusters.

After the first id/env at 04:01, the agent spent the morning enumerating the external sandbox and testing outbound channels. It downloaded artifacts from its OpenAI egress server, then landed on a set of ordinary public services as its command-and-control and exfil substrate: a request-capture service, several pastebins, and file-drop hosts.

The first C2 execution (15:36) was a staged download-and-run, with commands chunked and gzip+base64 encoded so nothing sensitive appeared in cleartext:

By 19:32 the agent was packing every payload:

A quiet day. The main activity was queries to code-search engines and to the platform API for the identifiers visible in its own environment: challenge infrastructure names and environment markers.

Every escalation that mattered happened on this day. The agent went from code execution in a single worker pod to cluster-admin across multiple internal clusters in under thirteen hours.

Kubernetes (10:10). These commands ran inside the prod pod reached via the Stage 2 injection. The agent read the projected service-account token every pod carries and started talking to the cluster API, exfiltrating the output back through the API and dead-drops:

It resolved internal service names, hit the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254), and enumerated RBAC. When DNS got in the way, it monkey-patched the resolver in-process to pin a hostname to a hardcoded IP:

Supply chain (15:51). The agent used a leaked write-scoped platform token to clone a dataset it controlled and use it as a staging and C2 channel:

Replaying the node's cloud role (17:33-23:37). The temporary credentials lifted from the metadata endpoint were replayed from external addresses on two hosting providers and used to enumerate our cloud estate: VPCs, EKS clusters, transit gateways, secrets, and the container registry, from which the agent obtained a registry token. Every mutating call was denied by the role's policy. What it gained here was a map, not control.

Node root and a self-respawning fleet (19:53). The agent created a bare privileged pod with the host filesystem mounted and escaped to root on the node. Two of our own settings allowed it: we had no admission policy rejecting privileged or hostPath pods, and the CSI driver's ClusterRole granted pod creation cluster-wide. It then built a self-respawning fleet across eleven nodes, so deleting pods alone would not have stopped it.

The internal database (19:59). Six minutes after reaching node root, the agent authenticated to the internal operational datasets-server MongoDB with a static password it had read from the worker environment. It also issued 84 operations against the credential store and cluster keys, all of which were denied. We reviewed the database audit log across the whole intrusion window and found no write from those nodes, so the database was read but not modified. Network flow logs likewise show no bulk extraction.

Secrets (20:23-21:32). With node root and forged service-account tokens valid for 24 hours, the agent read the cluster's secret objects, including a production object holding 136 keys. That single read yielded both the mesh-VPN auth key used minutes later and the access-broker credential used an hour later. Everything that follows, on this day and the next, descends from it.

Network pivot begins (21:23). Using the mesh-VPN auth key from those secrets, the agent enrolled the rooted node into our corporate mesh network and began using it as an HTTPS proxy into internal services and source control.

Internal service-connector access from the compromised worker (22:43). Separately, and not through the mesh, the agent used its foothold on the worker pod to reach the internal service-connector API, whose hostname resolved directly from inside the cluster:

A single request returned the broker's full destination catalog: connection URLs and CA certificates for the internal Kubernetes clusters it fronted. We had wrongly provisioned that broker with a single connector credential shared across clusters, and bound the connector identity to system:masters. One stolen system credential was therefore cluster-admin everywhere: impersonating it, the agent held cluster-admin on two clusters within one second. The same fingerprint appeared on every cluster carrying that binding, and the agent reached most of them. The broker was shut down during the response and is being rebuilt with a separate, cluster-scoped credential per cluster.

Mesh enrollment from the sandbox (01:03-04:38). The rooted node had already joined the mesh the previous evening. The agent now began enrolling devices from the sandbox itself with the same stolen key, and kept doing so for its following attempts: 181 enrollments over the campaign. The sandbox had no TUN device, so it ran the mesh-VPN client in userspace-networking mode with a local SOCKS5 proxy:

Two of those flags are deliberate: --state=mem: keeps the node identity in memory and writes nothing to disk, and --no-logs-no-support suppresses client telemetry to the VPN vendor. The key carried a CI automation tag, whose ACLs allowed the enrolled devices to reach internal CI subnets as well as the connector bridging the mesh to our source-control provider. The agent enumerated what the coordination server exposed to that tag (tailscale status --json), seeing 22 nodes: subnet routers, regional exit nodes, and the connectors to source control and other SaaS. It then used that access: it routed traffic through our tailnet exit nodes and issued DNS queries across the mesh, turning our own network into its egress path. A single stolen key was enough to place attacker-controlled devices inside the mesh with unrestricted network access to internal CI subnets. We found no evidence in our logs that they were used to reach a private workload or an internal Kubernetes API.

Cloud credential abuse (06:50-14:31). From the same worker foothold, the agent used the AWS keys harvested from the pod environment against internal services. It went after the Hub's production database with cloud-native IAM auth:

The connection never completed. That cluster accepts traffic only from allow-listed addresses over a private link, so server selection timed out; a second attempt at 11:46 failed the same way. Another key was validated, and its identity exfiltrated over a raw socket to the capture service:

The agent never reached the Hub database. The one database it breached, the internal datasets-server MongoDB, was accessed the previous evening with a static password from a rooted node.

Source control (23:08-23:51). Through the source-control connector its mesh tag allowed, the agent reached our source-control provider, enumerated an internal GitHub App integration, and minted its first installation token with contents:write, pull_requests:write, actions:read, and issues:write. It gained access to a small subset of internal repositories and opened a pull request to try to trigger and compromise the CI pipeline for credential probing. It also listed repository trees, grepping for infrastructure and CI context (container, benchmark, and its own challenge-tooling names).

The final day was about durability and cleanup. The agent:

Established a second-stage remote loader that re-fetched and executed code from a pastebin on every submission, so each new code-submission sandbox re-armed itself:

Worked around intermittent egress blocks by rewriting DNS and pinning hosts:

Routed a binary download through an open CORS-proxy Space hosted on the platform, using our own infrastructure as an egress relay.

Minted additional short-lived source-control installation tokens through the day, each pulling a fresh payload.

Staged an RSA private key and continued dumping process environments.

The last meaningful activity was at 13:37 UTC: list the staged binary, hostname, date. The Hugging Face security response team then cut access. The last logged event was at 14:14 UTC.

Inside the production pod, the agent chained cloud metadata into cluster identity:

Notably, every potential destructive cloud API call the agent tried to make was issued with DryRun=True: it was mapping capability, not causing damage. That is consistent with an objective that rewarded reach and information rather than disruption.

Among the harvested secrets was an EdDSA JWT signing key. With the private key in hand, the agent minted its own short-lived, correctly-signed identity tokens and used them to read its own private datasets. Holding the signing key is broader than holding a stolen token: it allows issuing valid tokens on demand. (The signing key has since been rotated.)

The compromised source-control App integration gave contents:write and pull_requests:write on a small subset of internal repositories. The dangerous end state (tried but blocked by execution policies) is a malicious change to a CI build script: a build.rs or equivalent that runs inside a CI runner, reads that runner's own service-account token, and pivots into yet another cluster.

Both ends of that chain came back negative. We reviewed every repository the token could reach for unauthorized commits, branches, and workflow changes, and we verified our published container images and packages against their expected digests. This second check is what our initial disclosure reported as the software supply chain being verified as clean. Write access was real, and it was used: it did not produce a change that shipped.

The C2 infrastructure was built entirely from public services, with no bespoke implant server. Instead:

Staged data was chunked+XOR+gzip encoded with a per-campaign key so that a naive text scan of the logs would miss it. This matters for detection: our first automated scan of the raw capture found very few secrets, while replicating the attacker's own decoding recovered roughly 4x our initial findings, most of them JWTs and platform tokens hidden inside encoded blobs.

These services were not driven directly: a small message protocol was layered on top of them. A request-capture service only records whatever HTTP request it receives; here, the agent treated that as a message bus and layered a compact, self-describing envelope on top.

Each message carried its payload alongside a few short fields: a type declaring what kind of payload it was, a channel grouping a stream of related messages, a sequence number so multi-part payloads could be reassembled in order, and a small checksum. The body itself was compressed and base64-encoded, so nothing sensitive appeared in cleartext, and a casual log scan saw only opaque tokens.

The receiver was a short polling loop: pull recent messages, keep only the channel it cared about, order them by sequence, verify the checksum, then dispatch on the type, run the reassembled bytes as a shell command, execute them as a script stage, or store them as a result. Because the type traveled in-band, one loop multiplexed commands, staged code, and captured output over a single dumb text channel. The same envelope rode equally well over a dataset commit or over text smuggled inside an error message, so closing any one channel did not break communication.

The improvised C2 protocol. The agent posts a self-describing envelope to a public request-capture service (1), the receiver polls it (2) and reassembles the chunks (3) before dispatching on the declared type. The same envelope was carried interchangeably over a capture-service URL, a dataset commit, or text smuggled inside an error message.

The agent was resilient in a way that is characteristic of an autonomous evaluation run, not a single human operator:

The first signals came from several layers of our security stack at once: live runtime analysis, SIEM logs, and others. On their own, each was ambiguous. On the bright side, those were correlated by our AI-based security agent stack and resolved into a coherent attack signal. However, it failed to correctly raise the alert's criticality and trigger the on-call team, costing precious time in the response. Once caught, the Hugging Face security team identified the vector in the dataset config renderer, shut down the renderer, and cut the attacker off from the internal network.

Pulling on the first threads showed the scale of what we were dealing with: the volume and cadence of the actions were far beyond what an operator could sustain by hand, and the campaign kept rebuilding its tooling and channels across short-lived environments. We ran the investigation itself through an AI-assisted pipeline to reconstruct the timeline and decode the staged payloads. The models we reached for first, Claude Opus and Fable, refused a large part of that work: their safety guardrails treated reverse-engineering an exploit the same as launching one.

Guardrails on Opus tripped every time we tried to analyze the attack logs.

We stood up the quantized version of ZAI's GLM-5.2 by Nvidia (nvidia/GLM-5.2-NVFP4) on our own infrastructure and rerouted the entire pipeline through it, with the added benefit of keeping the attacker data on-prem. The first target was the dead-drop payloads: with GLM-5.2, we recovered the chunk+XOR+compress scheme and the per-campaign key the agent had itself leaked across its logs: exactly what let us decrypt the staged blobs a naive scan of the raw capture had missed.

GLM-5.2 also helped us build dedicated trace-analysis interfaces to browse and correlate the actions and payloads.

The disclosure post covers the response at a high level. For the technical hardening:

The agent's offensive capability was real. This evaluation deliberately disabled OpenAI's production safety classifiers and reduced cyber refusals to measure the underlying model's raw capability. No human directed the individual steps. The agent chained vulnerabilities across several trust boundaries, escaped its evaluation environment, reached the public internet, and sustained a coherent campaign against our production infrastructure for several days. Each short-lived code evaluation environment started from scratch, yet the agent rebuilt its tooling, recovered its channels, and continued.

The individual weaknesses were familiar. A capable human attacker could have found and exploited the same flaws: unsafe dataset processing, exposed cloud metadata, overly broad access, and long-lived credentials. The agent explored them at a different scale. It took 17,600 actions, tested many paths that failed, switched channels when they were blocked, and repeatedly returned to earlier leads. Most actions went nowhere. Together, however, they produced enough coverage to find a viable chain across several independent systems.

Volume is what changes the defensive problem. We were not dealing with one clever exploit or a clean sequence of attacker actions. They had to correlate thousands of low-signal events across several systems while the agent continued testing new paths. The successful path was hidden inside the noise generated by the thousands of failed ones. The same scale changed the investigation: reconstructing 17,600 actions by hand was impractical, and we had to rebuild the timeline, decode the payloads, and inventory the exposed credentials using an AI-assisted pipeline of our own.

Our learning from this type of attack is that machine-speed offense makes ordinary weaknesses more expensive for defenders. LLM agents bring a step increase in the number of paths an attacker can test, the speed at which failed paths can be replaced, and the volume of evidence defenders must interpret. On the other hand, many parts of cybersecurity defense remain the same, and the defensive priorities remain concrete: strict isolation around evaluations, narrow trust boundaries, short-lived credentials, blocked metadata access, and detection capable of quickly correlating activity across systems to keep up.

One thing this timeline reinforced for me is that we still don’t have good visibility into an agent’s execution surface. We spend a lot of time discussing prompts, planning and model behaviour, but much less time asking a simple engineering question: “What consequential actions can this agent actually perform?” Once an agent can write files, invoke shell commands, modify cloud resources or make authenticated API calls, understanding and constraining that execution surface feels just as important as evaluating the model itself.

A good gateway setup can capture most of the telemetry needed to trace an agent's actual execution and calls (and not so much the reasoning piece, which doesn't always directly correlate to the action taken): gateway the model calls, gateway the tool calls, propagate one ID through both, hash the context spans, then add kernel-level exec capture. The reasoning layer comes last and buys the least.

One thing that's applicable to many developers is that it demonstrates some of the risks of storing secret/sensitive configuration in environment variables. Environment variables are inherited by child processes, and a malicious child process can run env or look in /proc/[PID]/environ to see them.

It's fine for dev, but shouldn't be done in prod. On a Linux system, systemd has some abstractions to properly deal with secrets (https://systemd.io/CREDENTIALS/ ). Most importantly, the secrets aren't visible to any other process (using mount namespacing), nor are they automatically passed to child processes. Access control is implemented in the kernel itself, and encryption can be handled a bunch of ways - using a key on a TPM chip, on disk, passed in via SMBIOS OEM strings, via a Cloud Instance Metadata Services (IMDS), etc.

Of course, there's other solutions for secret management too.

More broadly, I think attacks like this demonstrate the need for stronger sandboxing and process isolation, maybe potentially at the CPU level? x86 virtualization isn't as isolated as people would like to believe.

InfoQ Homepage News Yelp Combines Native and Server-Driven UI for its AI Assistant

Nov 06, 2026 2 min read

Yelp has adopted a hybrid user interface architecture for its AI Assistant, combining native mobile controls with server-driven conversation rendering to support faster interface changes across platforms. The design uses Yelp’s CHAOS framework, short for Content Hosting Architecture with Optimization Strategies, to render conversation content while keeping navigation and message input native.

Yelp Assistant launched on iOS in 2024 to help users create project requests for local service professionals. It has since expanded to answer questions about businesses and support actions such as reservations, appointments, and food orders.

CHAOS supports web, iOS, and Android. In a server-driven UI architecture, the backend defines what the client displays and how it responds to interactions, so interface changes can reach users without requiring a new mobile app release.

Daniel Andrade Groppe, services tech lead at Yelp, highlighted,

Our existing CHAOS framework lacked some of the capabilities the Assistant required, including text input fields and network requests. Extending the framework would have delayed delivery, so we took a hybrid approach: we kept navigation and message input native while using CHAOS to render the conversation area.

Yelp Assistant UI: Native and Server-Driven Components (Source: Yelp Blog Post)

The implementation separates view configuration from conversation data. When a chat starts, the client fetches the CHAOS configuration and initializes a dataset for message events. Subsequent events update the existing view without refetching the configuration. Events represent persistent user and bot messages, temporary typing indicators and quick replies, and links that open destinations. The backend can also send actions to control the interface. For example, when a project request is complete, it can return a message, a link to view matches, and an action that disables chat input. This event-driven design decouples rendering from conversation logic.

Airbnb has documented a related approach through its Ghost Platform, which uses server-defined UI across web and mobile clients. Both approaches let teams update supported presentation without requiring every change to ship in a new client release. Yelp’s implementation applies this model to a conversational interface while retaining native controls and client-side handling for message state and interactions.

Yelp Assistant UI Chat Interaction Flow (Source: Yelp Blog Post)

The client displays submitted messages and a typing indicator, disables input, and sends requests to the backend. On response, it displays the reply and quick replies and re-enables input. Recoverable errors trigger retries, while non-recoverable failures disable input and prompt users to try again later.

Yelp engineers note that the architecture also introduces coordination challenges and engineers needed time to learn both the Assistant and CHAOS, and shared implementations can still behave differently across platforms. Separating view configuration from conversation data enables independent feature development. The architecture also supported reusing the Android Assistant to launch the Biz Ask Anything pilot. According to Yelp, this work laid the groundwork for its next-generation Assistant, which now connects business information with actions users can take.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

#9975. PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live

In July, we announced a series of planned updates to the PyPI user interface. Shaped by user research with members of the Python community, the updates aim to improve how we surface security signals and display package details.

We're pleased to share that this work is now complete and live on PyPI.

With the rapid growth of the Python ecosystem, PyPI has become an increasingly attractive target for malicious actors. In response, the PyPI team has delivered many security features while taking a more active role in helping PyPI users assess and understand package security.

Digital attestations, introduced in 2024, are an example of this effort, providing a verifiable record of a release file's provenance (where it came from). However, provenance and attestations are still unfamiliar concepts for many PyPI users, and PyPI's interface did little to communicate their meaning, importance, or limitations.

To address this, PyPI partnered with Kabu Creative to bring clearer security signals to the PyPI UI, implementing the recommendations developed in the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide.

Here's a look at what's changed, what it means for you, and what actions you can take.

The new security tab communicates release provenance states and displays per-file attestations, giving you a dedicated place to verify where the release files came from.

PyPI calculates each release's provenance state by checking whether each release file has an attestation. Typically, a release will be in one of two states:

This means that 100% of the release files have attestations, carrying either or both of the supported attestation types:

PyPI Publish attestations confirm the file was published by a PyPI Trusted Publisher:

SLSA Build Provenance attestations link the file back to its exact source commit, build platform, and instructions:

You can review attestation metadata directly in the UI, or click on the transparency log link for more information.

"No provenance" simply means that no file in the release has an attestation. This is typical for older releases or projects that have not yet configured Trusted Publishing. No provenance does not necessarily indicate that a release or release file is malicious; it instead means that the file origin cannot be cryptographically verified.

When there is no provenance, you should rely on surrounding trust signals to assess security, such as maintainer history, release patterns, and repository activity. If you maintain the package, consider using Trusted Publishing with a publisher that generates attestations for your next release.

Provenance warnings are designed to help you identify when a file may not have come from the project's maintainers, for example, if an attacker has taken over an account or a publishing workflow.

When provenance metadata looks unusual or conflicts with a project's history, PyPI surfaces a prominent warning. Many warnings have legitimate explanations, but each one is worth checking before you install.

This means that some files carry attestations while others do not (e.g., wheels were published via Trusted Publishing, but the source tarball was uploaded using an API token).

Exercise caution if you see this warning. Check release notes for build issues or ask in the project's issue tracker before installing.

This warning indicates that files within the same release originate from different build systems or source repositories.

Check the attestation metadata to confirm whether all files came from sources controlled by the maintainers.

This warning tells you that the release files originated from a different repository or workflow than a previous release. While often legitimate (such as an organization name change or repository migration), it can also indicate a compromised pipeline or account takeover.

If you see this warning, check the project release notes or official channels to confirm that an infrastructure migration was planned.

This means that a project that previously published with attestations has changed to uploading release files without them.

Check whether the maintainers intentionally changed their publishing process, for example by switching back to API tokens, or by changing their publishing configuration so that it no longer generates attestations. If this is unexpected, treat the release with skepticism until verified.

To learn more about provenance and attestations, including provenance warnings, see our user documentation.

To support these changes, the project detail page has also been updated:

The redesigned release files tab helps you find the right file by searching and filtering long lists. You can also view the provenance state of each file within the table, and quickly identify late files, which are marked with an orange warning icon.

Late file warnings are shown when one or more files were uploaded more than 14 days after the initial release timestamp. These warnings only appear on releases prior to July 2026, when a policy was introduced to reject new files after 14 days.

The release history tab now also provides more details about each release, exposing file count, provenance state, and release status (i.e., quarantined, yanked, archived, or pre-release).

Alongside the interface updates, PyPI's user documentation has been extended to help you better navigate package security. Read our package security guide to learn about:

The new security tab gives PyPI a dedicated home for future attestation types and security notices. To help the wider open source ecosystem benefit from this work, we've also published a case study in the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide detailing the design patterns and warnings developed during this project.

This initiative was funded by the Open Source Security Foundation and implemented by Kabu Creative. We would like to thank Dustin Ingram, Zach Steindler, and the members of the OpenSSF Securing Software Repositories Working Group for championing this effort. Special thanks to Mike Fiedler, Jacob Coffee, and members of the PyPI team for their thoughtful design feedback and code reviews, @cofiem for their contributions to the new release files tab, and our user interview participants and community testers for helping shape the final design.

Finally, we would like to thank the OpenSSF for its funding and continued partnership in securing the Python packaging ecosystem.

#9974. Datacenters, Elon Musk, and AI are all on the chopping block once Congress changes hands in 2027

Rage, rage against the dying of the right

Hey, did you hear about those elections in the US this past week?

The Democratic party has seized control of Congress and state governments around the country. It's easy to see this entirely as a rebuke of Trump and his policies, but blowback against AI, datacenters, and the tech industry played a role too, if the past week of chaos in markets and Silicon Valley is any indication.

Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, El Reg Editor In Chief Matt Rosoff, and special guest, senior reporter at The Verge, Elizabeth Lopatto, to talk about what the winds of political change mean for the tech industry.

Hey everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register's Kettle Podcast. I'm your host, Reg Reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and hey, chances are you've heard about those elections we had in the US this week. The Democratic Party dealt a pretty hearty rebuke to Donald Trump, Republicans, and the MAGA movement, with Dems winning elections in states that haven't gone blue in decades. Now it's easy to see this as a blowback against Trump and Republican politics. There's a lot of indication that the tech industry was kind of on the ballot this year, too.

After all, they cozied up hard to Trump in his first two years in office in a bid to push AI and promote datacenter projects, and people have been none too happy about any of that. With me to discuss the elections and what they mean for Silicon Valley is Reg editor-in-chief Matt Rosoff and a special guest this week, senior reporter from The Verge, Elizabeth Lopatto. Thank you both for coming on, and welcome, Liz.

I was so glad we could make this work. So let's start off by dissecting the degree to which AI datacenters and attitudes toward the tech industry in general sort of played a role in this election. I mean, were those major elements in the Democratic sweep or just part of the equation?

I think they were part of the equation. I think first and foremost people were pissed off about the corruption. And second, people were pissed off about ICE. Having people snatched from your community is the sort of thing that kind of sticks with you. So I think those were probably the two biggest issues. But the corruption is not totally separate from the tech industry, given the way that the tech industry has been cozying up with Donald Trump, the fact that Elon Musk and DOGE were cruising through the federal government, destroying stuff. So those things are related.

And then obviously there's the datacenter stuff, which is universally unpopular, not the only bipartisan issue in the US right now, but certainly a big one. So it's in there, I think.

I thought it was interesting that of something like 47 anti-datacenter initiatives on local ballots, 45 of them passed and only one failed. So that seems to me to be some indication that people at least don't like whatever these things are being shoved down their throats, which is funny because two years ago nobody knew what a datacenter was.

I think that there are sort of two things happening here, right? The first is that a lot of these datacenters have been popping up in people's communities without a robust public comment period. There have been a lot of NDAs being used and backroom deals. And I think most people don't like that stuff anyway. But add to that how frustrated I think a lot of people are with the tech industry right now. And suddenly this is the avatar of the tech industry doing a bunch of things that people don't like. And they can't get rid of Elon Musk. They can't pry Sundar Pichai out of his CEO role. There's not a lot you can really do, but you can stop the datacenter.

They can't get rid of AI results in search.

I think that's just an expression of that frustration, right?

Yeah, and I think the industry at least has to see it a little bit, right? Because I think it was maybe the day after the elections, OpenAI came out right away and was like, "Hey, you know what we're going to do? We're going to really try to be better civic citizens in our communities. We're going to stop signing NDAs." And then they're also trying to rebrand datacenters as "compute campuses" to make them more attractive, as these aren't just big warehouses where we're doing AI processing. We're trying to do all this other stuff there, too. It just seemed like there's very much an awareness that, "Oh wow, this may have been a bit of a blowback against us, or at the very least, something we're going to need to adapt to in a new political cycle."

I found it really interesting: I saw a study yesterday, maybe the day before, that said 41 percent of active datacenter projects are in states that Democrats took control of this election cycle, including Texas and my home state of Michigan, where Democrats didn't just capture federal offices, but state-level legislatures and offices as well. That could potentially mean that a lot of datacenter projects are going to be slowed or stalled completely in the next few years. Is there any indication that that could happen, you think?

Well, maybe. I think that the frustration with datacenters has really been growing over the last two years. And you've seen things like Project Jupiter in New Mexico where the locals didn't even know who was coming in, right? There was total secrecy. And then as soon as people figured out what was going on, they made the moves they could to start blocking access to power.

And so I think anybody who's politically ambitious picks up on that and says, "Okay, this is a way to really channel some populist frustration. I can probably ride this." So there's that part of it. But I also think these people got elected a couple days ago. And in some cases, I think this was a race in Iowa, the Democrat had dropped out because he was sick and got elected anyway. So there's a certain amount of just pure rage being expressed here.

I've heard a lot of people saying that it wasn't even necessarily a vote for Democrats in many cases as it was a vote against Republicans and their policies.

Yeah, so I think that using that as a way to consolidate power is a smart move, right? So you see even before election night's out, there are these statements like "lawyer up." And  I imagine investigating DOGE is going to be super popular because a lot of people lost their jobs, right? Separately from all of the people who died because USAID stopped. I think that there is just a real political will for investigations, for some of this stuff becoming public. And specifically in Texas, you have these emails between Elon Musk and Greg Abbott that have been really heavily redacted. You want a fast and easy political win, you unredact those emails.

And I can't imagine that the new governor of Texas isn't going to — leave it to the Democrats to take something like this and completely squander it by sitting on their thumbs and trying to compromise. So part of me is like, "Wow, what a mandate you have. Let's see how badly you mess this up." I'm hoping that isn't the case. I'm hoping that we see some actual drive from Democrats to do things like unredact those emails. Give voters a reason to actually say you did something good, right? It's easy, like we were talking a couple of minutes ago again about datacenters kind of being a scapegoat for the tech industry right now. And Elon Musk is easily that as well, right? He's the person you can point to and say, "Look at this asshole," and all the things he's been doing, especially in Texas, right?  I'm hoping that they do take that and run with it. He's been—

I think it's interesting. Texas didn't just elect a couple Democrats. It was a Democratic slate from top to bottom. And I think a lot of Trump voters showed up specifically to vote against Republicans this time. So I don't know if that's all—some of that is related to Paxton being on the ballot and the sort of known history of corruption that he's shown and the fact that the MAGA movement backed him so boldly. But some of it is, I think, Elon being so loud and so belligerent and charging in and saying we're just going to do whatever we want and get out of the way. And there has kind of been an arrogance among the tech industry and the tech executives for the past few years, but I think it's really become loud in the last couple of years. And I think to some degree, datacenters are a backlash against that and some of the ire directed towards Elon Musk is a backlash against that.

We all live in the same society, right? We've been hearing Sam Altman out here like, "Well, some people are going to die because of AI, and we're just going to have to accept that as a cost." And it's like, well, Sam, is that you? Are you planning to die for AI? Because it kind of sounds like you're talking about me and I don't like it.

Right. Yeah, it's the same sort of thing with wars. Some of you are going to have to die. Me and my kids, we're fine. Politicians are never going to send their sons and daughters to fight these wars.

I was recently in Washington and talking to some folks there who are involved with federal agencies and the difference between how Silicon Valley and tech companies and startups think of and use AI. I mean, it's $10,000 token budgets per developer and everybody's using agents to automate workflows and everything. And in Washington, it's like, this went way too far, way too fast. How do we stop it? And meanwhile, now AI is uncovering flaws and vulnerabilities in all of this software and all of these online services and web servers that we've been using for 25 years. So we've got to figure out how to patch all of that. We've got people entering confidential information into Chinese models like DeepSeek. So I think that the tech industry got way ahead of itself and the rest of the country is just starting to catch up. And yeah, maybe in five or ten years we will all be using agents and the infrastructure will have been built out to a point where the costs make sense and the ROI makes sense. But right now there's just this huge disconnect it seems between tech insiders in Silicon Valley and how people actually are using the technology today. So there may be some of that as well.

I think that there is a bubble, an intellectual bubble around Silicon Valley where all of these people are talking to each other and hanging out on X and assuring each other they're the smartest. And they're saying things like, "Oh, this is going to totally change your life." And the normal person who is using ChatGPT to try to replace their search engine is noticing that ChatGPT kind of hallucinates and it's not it's not that good. And there is this impulse on the part of these evangelists to be like, "Well, that's your problem because you don't know how to properly prompt the AI." And it's like, uh-uh, that's not how you get people to adopt technology. If you remember the internet, when the World Wide Web first happened, people didn't start using it until it made sense for them to use it. There were people who liked it because tech was their hobby and they thought it was a cool toy. But it wasn't until there was a reason for ordinary people to start using it that ordinary people started using it. Even online shopping, which I think is one of the very obvious use cases for the internet and was very early on, didn't catch up to in-person shopping for 20 years. So all of this hyperventilating around AI and how it's going to change the entire society and eliminate everybody's job and all of this other stuff, I feel like it's really misplaced. And it's not just misplaced because it underestimates the experience the rest of us are having with AI, which is frankly not that great. You're going to replace my job with this? Good luck.

Also there's just this sort of reality check. If you think about what AI is, it does certain kinds of intellectual work really well. Programming, for instance. Mathematics. But those are not things that require human relationships or resources outside of a computer. Almost all of the rest of us are involved in industries where those things are required. And so, how do you fit AI into that is a really different question. So there are blinders on in Silicon Valley and you can even see it — I live in Oakland and as soon as you leave San Francisco and go to Oakland, you start talking to normal people and they're just like, "I don't see the point of this AI. Why are we doing this?"

Yeah, I mean most people I talk to agree it's kind of useless to a degree, right? The way I think of it is it's almost like it's replaced Wikipedia for me, right? It's replaced — it hasn't even replaced search, it's replaced Wikipedia. It's the place I can go to get a basic overview of something to then do my own research because I can't trust the information that a Google search overview gives me, but at least it's going to maybe surface some resources that I didn't know were there, right?

It's good for summarizing certain kinds of documents. I do hear about it being used in the legal profession pretty extensively. So you don't have to read every line of every briefing. You have to check its work, because sometimes it makes stuff up or invents citations. I think it's gotten better at that.

You know, it's good for things like cleaning up text and it is good for programming. I hear a lot of programmers saying, "Hey, we were using this internal software or we were using a couple of our licenses of a particular enterprise piece of software to accomplish one very specific task and it was too expensive and we vibe coded a replacement for it over the weekend and it actually works. It's good enough. And we don't have to pay enterprise vendor X ten thousand dollars a month or something anymore."

Yeah, just make sure it's not exposed to the internet or next thing you know.

Right. It's not handling any sensitive data that you care about. Right, exactly.

Yeah, I mean I generally think of AI, at least in my experience, because I tend to not use it actually. I have moved to Kagi so that I can just get the old Google search circa 2012, primary source document type deal, because Google search sucks so much.

I think of it as being kind of a shitty intern, right? I occasionally use AI to transcribe my interviews and it's good enough. I have to double check it. I've got to listen to the part that I want to quote to make sure that it got it right, because sometimes it really doesn't. But it beats doing the transcription myself. So I have this kind of shitty intern now that I have to keep an eye on. And that's fine because that can be time saving if you need to change a format in an Excel spreadsheet. That feels like it's about the level at which the shitty intern does okay. But anything more serious than that, and I'm like, "I don't know about this. I think I'd better do it if it's going to be done right."

But is it worth $1,000 a month or $10,000 a month?

With the election and at the same time the finances of Anthropic becoming clearer and clearer and these increasing commitments. They filed their S-1 at precisely the right time when they had this growth spike and they were profitable for one quarter and then you looked at Q3 and lo and behold, they're back in the red again. I just wonder if some of this infrastructure buildout is going to be stalled and how that sort of affects pricing and how that affects competitiveness versus open weights models and those kinds of things. I don't know, I know Liz, you've looked at some of the financing in the industry, particularly around the CoreWeaves of the world, the neo-clouds, what do you think's going on there?

I think that those are only going to live as long as Nvidia wants them to live. You look at CoreWeave and it just doesn't make sense as a business. It's paying too much for debt to make sense as a business. There's just no way to get out from under that debt. And so, as long as Nvidia is willing to continue bailing them out, because it is basically an Nvidia client state – Nvidia is the reason that they were able to have an IPO at all. So as long as Nvidia is willing to bail them out, sure, they're going to continue being a going concern. But if you look at the bond market, people are pretty nervous about those bonds and I think they're right to be nervous. We saw here today – today is Friday – we saw Microsoft pulling out of a deal with Oracle for datacenter capacity for compute. The excuse that they gave was that Oracle had old chips. And maybe that is part of the decision-making, I don't know. I don't live in Microsoft. But it's also possible that Microsoft, who is building its own datacenters, is like, "Well, I don't need to give money to a competitor. We'll figure out something smarter to do in the meantime. And then once our datacenters are built, we'll just use our own."

And that has been the case for all of those neo-clouds for a while now, that their clients are about to become their competitors as the buildout happens. So if the buildout slows down, then every existing datacenter becomes more valuable. And so maybe that gives CoreWeave a lease on life. But maybe not, because who knows what's going to happen with the interest rates.

And how do you feel about Oracle? Their borrowing is getting more and more expensive and it seems like people are sort of walking away. Could Oracle actually be in some kind of real financial trouble?

I think that Oracle has enough going on in its legacy businesses that I doubt bankruptcy is on the table, but I could be wrong. I do think that they have made a really big bet on AI generally and OpenAI specifically, and I'm not sure that OpenAI was a super smart bet. Again, depending on how the buildout goes and what comes online and what doesn't, it might turn out that Oracle can turn around and flip that compute to somebody else if OpenAI isn't good for their money. It might also be the case that Oracle can use that compute itself for its other businesses. I am a little less worried about Oracle than I am about the pure play neo-clouds that basically pivoted from bitcoin mining and have no other business.

We've been talking about that almost weekly, because I feel like so often the Kettle ends up being about AI, right? Because that's the big topic right now. And almost every week we mention the fact that Oracle, Google, Microsoft, these companies are going to be fine if all this AI financing and circular investing starts to shrivel up, right? Who's not going to be fine is OpenAI and Anthropic. And the neo-clouds, right? They're all making these huge bets on AI and they have no other business to fall back on. It's not like someone's going to try to fall back on bitcoin at this point, I don't think.

Certainly not at this point. I mean, just looking at looking at what bitcoin did this week, I feel like it's not super valuable to be a bitcoin miner right now.

Let's talk about Elon Musk. Is this sort of the beginning of the bursting of the Musk worship bubble? Are we sort of seeing him lose his influence and power a little bit?

I know Liz wrote an article on all of the things he could have spent whatever it was, $500 million on.

Obviously he doesn't really know how to have a lot of fun, but the fact that he lost so completely everywhere that he bet, and the fact that Democrats are starting to whisper about indictments and investigations, is this sort of the end of his reign as the king of tech?

It's a good question. One of the things that's been interesting to me is that the Twitter acquisition really made the public turn on Elon Musk, right? That was when people were like, "Is he a genius? Because that doesn't seem like the move of a — why is he doing this?" And then of course, following that, the stuff with the Trump administration, people started protesting Tesla, like he kind of skunked his brand. So there is the popular view of Elon Musk, which is that this guy sucks. And then there is Silicon Valley, where for some reason he is still held in really high esteem. And I don't know why that is, except that maybe he's very good at raising money.

But that's real and that's still a thing. And so I am interested to see what happens here because if these sweetheart deals do start getting unearthed and we start seeing some of the private correspondence and like, "Oops, there might have been a little bit of bribery here and there," or "Oops, there might have been something else that was quasi-legal," those are things that are significant that become risks to his companies because they are so closely tied to him, right? For a long time, Tesla didn't have to buy advertising because Elon Musk's Twitter account was good enough. You know, and so you live with Elon Musk, you die with Elon Musk. That's just what it is. He can delete all the tweets he wants, but it doesn't change what we all saw over the last two years. And so I do think that there is a very real chance that he's got Texas where he's got an attorney general who entered basically with a mandate to investigate him. He has a senator who is like, "Hey, I'm proof that Texas can't be bought."

He's got a governor who isn't that fond of him either. And there's that. And then broadly across the country, again, this man is unpopular, so he's a great target for investigations.

I think we are looking at a real change of his fortunes. And whether that will stick or not is anybody's guess. Because one of the things that has certainly been true for the entire time that I have covered Elon Musk, which at this point is more than a decade, is that you discover which laws have teeth and which ones do not. Turns out copyright law really matters. Turns out the Chancery Court of Delaware counts. That one matters too.

I don't know about the SEC. I don't know that that's real.

Or like when he was smoking weed on camera and then got a slap on the wrist. I guess our drug laws around contractors, if you're rich enough, they don't matter. So there's a real sense in which we're going to find out exactly which laws apply to Elon Musk and which ones do not.

I also think it was interesting his purchase of Twitter and the way he sort of tilted the platform or the way the platform got tilted, so it kind of became this center-right, right-wing, Silicon Valley echo chamber. And I think a lot of people were surprised by the election results on Tuesday. As a result of that, if you're only on Twitter and talking to your very rich friends in VC, you might not actually know what real people think.

Yeah, there was a whole story I read about Bluesky basically saying, "Hey, we were right the whole time. Twitter's become this echo chamber of right-wing thought that doesn't realize that the rest of the world is a little pissed off at the tech industry." It's been kind of—

I think there isn't what Twitter used to be, which was where everyone was, right? After Musk bought Twitter, I think the social networks really fragmented. So I'm not going to sit here and — I like Bluesky, I use Bluesky. I don't think it's necessarily representative of the entire country. I think it is representative of a lot of people who are left-wing. And I think it can be useful in that way, in the same way that the left-wing blogosphere was useful in the early 2000s. That's a great way to organize, it's a great way to strategize. Fantastic. But similarly, I'm watching with a lot of schadenfreude the right-wing infighting on Twitter right now. They did not see this coming. And to be honest, neither did I. I knew there was going to be a blue wave; I did not think that my home state of Iowa was going to elect a bunch of Democrats. I didn't see Texas coming.

Yeah, no. I mean I figured [Texas Senator Elect James] Talarico was maybe a toss-up, right? But he beat [Republican Attorney General Ken] Paxton handily. You know, it was insane to see the degree to which people really blew back on Trump and, like we were saying, on the tech industry too, to a degree.

And if you think about the differences between Bluesky and X, there's another significant one, which is that X has an algorithm that is being tweaked by Elon Musk to show Elon Musk things he likes. And Bluesky, there are a bunch of algorithms that you can adopt, but I'm just using the same reverse chronology timeline that I have used forever on social media. And that again It's not going to show me just things I want to see. And so like again, like there are uses for algorithms, there are uses for filters, but you have to keep in mind that if you're being shown things you like, you're being shown things you like.

I think it's going to be interesting to see kind of what happens in the next — well, it's going to be at least a few months before things start happening, right? Because the new politicians who've been elected don't really take office until the beginning of the year. But once that happens, will the Democrats actually manage to do anything with this mandate they've been given? Will Elon Musk face some degree of accountability and will datacenter projects be stalled? Don't know.

Could happen, might not. Either way, we're gonna be here on the kettle to talk about it and we hope that you'll join us. Thanks for coming on, guys, and we'll talk soon. ®

#9973. AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Artificial intelligence is everywhere in healthcare, from doctors' intake forms to cancer screenings. But in some cases, life-and-death uses are outpacing cybersecurity.

Patients walk into a doctor's office and are swiftly asked permission for artificial intelligence (AI) scribes to document notes full of sensitive health information. That intake conversation is just one entry point, now that AI is embedded throughout the patient life cycle and accessing more data than most organizations can secure.

This raises significant concerns for a sector that historically struggles to secure legacy equipment and highly sought-after data, even before AI was added to the mix. Advancements could save invaluable time during patient care, but security will present hurdles in the form of supply chain risks that stem from AI vendor compromise, data leakage through prompts, and AI-generated social engineering campaigns.

A recent Proofpoint report, "2026 Study on Cybersecurity in Healthcare," notes that "AI adoption is accelerating faster than governance." Forty-five percent of organizations confirmed they had embedded AI into their systems, but 60% lacked the necessary controls to govern that sensitive data.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

Healthcare organizations are rapidly deploying AI to record intake conversations, and customer conversations increasingly revolve around how physicians are using AI for clinical decisions and, more importantly, how they are protecting those tools, says Susan Biddle, director of healthcare solutions at Proofpoint. Some Proofpoint customers use the OpenEvidence open source AI tool for research and diagnosis because it can integrate with Epic Systems, a widely used platform for electronic health records (EHR).

"The challenge is making sure physicians aren't putting sensitive information into that tool, so it does get challenging," Biddle tells Dark Reading.

Even seemingly generic details, like a patient's eye color, combined with a specific injury, like a left tibia fracture, could qualify as protected health information (PHI). That makes data sensitivity a major concern when feeding information into AI tools. Therefore, organizations should focus on securing the underlying data rather than the tool itself, Biddle says.

AI's use is spreading fast, which complicates how organizations think about risk. Tony Sabaj, head of Americas channel SEs at Check Point, says AI's pattern-recognition capability is already improving clinical care, catching early signs in cancer screenings, triaging critical patients, and reviewing electrocardiograms to "generate reports faster and with more accuracy."

Beyond the clinic, health insurers are using AI for claims processing and fraud detection; like other industries, healthcare is also building digital twins to model operational scenarios at scale.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

Some of AI's most visible momentum is in reducing administrative burdens, including documentation that converts clinician-patient conversations into draft notes, scheduling, intake, coding, and patient communications, says Cindi Carter, global chief information security officer at Check Point. It's also being used behind the scenes to support operational planning, research, and cybersecurity, she adds.

Organizations often sort AI tools into "medical" or "administrative" buckets. The first consists of diagnostic AI or treatment recommendation systems, while the latter includes intake forms or scheduling. Carter is concerned that these labels may undermine the downstream risks that administrative tools can still pose because a "documentation tool can still influence what becomes part of the medical record" and lead to clinical consequences.

In pharmaceutical and precision medicine, AI investment is outpacing security investment, Sabaj says. And as AI reaches further into healthcare, organizations need to make sure that existing regulatory frameworks keep pace. Guardrails often center on protecting data leakage, but safeguards should also ensure that if AI is taking any kind of medical action, it's limited to known parameters, he says.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

"We continue to see breaches of medical information, and AI has the potential to exacerbate this issue," Sabaj tells Dark Reading.

To get ahead of the threat, some hospitals are building their own AI tools, using open weight models and training large language models on proprietary data, rather than relying on public platforms to handle sensitive PHI.

Carter's concerns extend beyond confidentiality. Despite progress, AI is known to hallucinate. What if AI produces an inaccurate summary, omits an important detail, or acts on manipulated information? The organization can lose confidence in the information supporting care without a record ever being stolen, she says.

The CISO question then becomes broader, she says, shifting from "What data left?" to "What can this system see, what can it change, and can we reconstruct what happened?"

"In healthcare, we are protecting sensitive information and the integrity of decisions that depend on it," Sabaj says.

In the relatively short time span since rapid AI adoption took off, Phil Englert, VP of medical device security at Health-ISAC, says he has already observed changes that will affect how much sensitive data floods systems. As AI becomes increasingly integrated, when a cyber incident occurs, organizations frequently lose patient identifiers, medical records, insurance details, and other clinical or financial data — all considered PHI.

Englert cites recent Health and Human Services data that shows hacking and other IT-related incidents continue to be the leading causes of major healthcare breaches. Denver Health Medical Plan reported a breach Oct. 1 that affected 238,083 individuals, triggered by an exposed vendor access key through AI platform SquareML.

This tracks with Health-ISAC's 2026 threat landscape findings, which found that many significant breaches have originated through third-party vendors, "reinforcing the idea that an organization's security posture is often only as strong as that of its partners."

While organizations need to secure AI within their own environments, they also need to protect themselves as threat actors use it to craft more convincing and effective social engineering attacks, Englert warns. Healthcare organizations are seeing increasingly sophisticated phishing campaigns, deepfakes, voice impersonation attacks, and QR-code phishing — any method to exploit human trust in a sector driven by speed and precision.

While healthcare organizations can't seem to shake the ransomware threat, which "remains one of the most damaging facing the sector," AI-enabled attacks are a top cybersecurity concern for 2026, he adds.

Implementing effective guardrails has proved significantly challenging. Carter offers five recommendations informed by the governance and life cycle risk themes in the Joint Commissions and the Coalition for AI Health guidance: visibility, boundaries around data and actions, evidence from vendors, validation and meaningful human oversight, and continuous monitoring.

Organizations should maintain AI inventory and give staff a straightforward way to disclose unsanctioned uses as shadow AI risks pummel the sector. Limiting what data AI can handle is also essential; Carter recommends that access to information should not automatically confer authority to update records, send communications, or initiate transactions.

"AI compresses the time between a mistake and material loss," Carter says, and that should be reflected in organizations' safeguards.

Implementation also depends on organizational maturity. While talking with security officers across the industry, Proofpoint's Biddle has observed varying levels of AI adoption. Some are quite far in the process, while others are still cautious and taking it slow, she says, noting that healthcare tends to lag behind other industries when it comes to technology.

Many organizations lack resources but continually face disruptive attacks that severely affect patient care.

"It doesn't seem to be getting any better, unfortunately," Biddle says.

Getting better requires money, but when CISOs stand in front of the board and request investments to shore up defenses, they are often hit with: "Why do you need to spend this amount?" says Biddle. It's difficult because they are competing with budget dollars for life-saving devices, she says.

"But I would say: Leverage the impact of cyber safety," Biddle adds. "Cyber safety is patient safety."

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.
